hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever said something out loud, and felt it change the room?
options: then you know what words can do. listen.
most of us have. this one is about that power. listen.
then listen. this story starts with a voice.

steps.line: The Torah opens with its first word, Bereshit: in the beginning. There was darkness over the deep, and the spirit of God hovering over the water.
Then God speaks, and that is all it takes. “Let there be light.” And there was light.

steps.q: Light comes on day one. When does the Torah say the sun is made?
steps.why: Light comes three days before the sun. The rabbis asked what that first light was; one teaching says God hid it away for the righteous.

steps.line: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” Not “the first day.” One day.

steps.q: Why might the Torah say “one day” and not “the first day”?
o: Nothing yet existed to count against
It was the only day God rested
Hebrew had no word yet for first
steps.why: One way to read it: there was nothing yet to count against. Rashi adds another: on that day, God was alone, the One, in the world.

steps.line: The rabbis tell a story. The Torah begins with bet, the second letter. So alef, the first letter, came to God and complained, for twenty-six generations.
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.q: Alef complains that it should have been first. What does God answer?
steps.why: God promised alef the first word at Sinai. And the words spoken there begin with alef.

steps.line: God said: when I give the Torah at Sinai, I’ll begin with you. And the words spoken at Sinai begin with alef: Anochi, “I am.”
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.q: Alef complained for twenty-six generations. Why that number?
o: From Adam to Sinai is 26 generations
steps.why: Count from Adam to Moses and you get twenty-six. Alef waited the whole way to Sinai. (Hebrew has twenty-two letters.)

steps.line: Today, Bereshit is read every autumn, right after the scroll is rolled back to the beginning. In this story, the world is made with words.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. the rabbis noticed bet is closed on three sides and open only toward the front, the way hebrew is read. one teaching says: what came before isn’t yours to chase. start here, and go forward.
and the world begins with a sentence. the rabbis said it was made with ten sayings. so words are never small. death and life, says an old proverb, are in the power of the tongue.

steps.q: If God made the world by speaking, what does the tradition suggest about your own words?
o: They can build or break a world
steps.why: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue,” says Proverbs. The rabbis took hurtful speech, lashon hara, very seriously.

today.say: today, notice one sentence before you say it, kind or sharp. choose the one that builds. that’s bereshit in a sentence: words make worlds.
options: one sentence that builds. that’s a whole new day.
good. noticing comes first, then the light.

tomorrow.title: The light that was hidden.
tomorrow.line: light on day one, but no sun until day four. so what was that first light, and where did it go?

sources: Genesis 1:1 (“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth,” JPS 1917); 1:2 (darkness upon the face of the deep, the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters); 1:3 (“And God said: ‘Let there be light.’ And there was light,” JPS 1917); 1:5 (“And there was evening and there was morning, one day,” JPS 1917)

Genesis Rabbah 1:10 (why the world was created with bet: closed on three sides, open in front; alef complains for twenty-six generations; at Sinai I will begin with you, Anochi; in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Avina, shortened)

Exodus 20:2 (Anochi, ‘I am’); Mishnah Avot 5:1 (ten sayings); Proverbs 18:21 (“Death and life are in the power of the tongue,” JPS 1917); Rashi on Genesis 1:5 and Genesis Rabbah 3:8 (‘one day’, not ‘first’: God was alone in His world)
check: The ‘nothing yet to count against’ reading of ‘one day’ is offered as one way to read it, beside Rashi’s; confirm the scholar is happy with it
